chapters.category: Aramaic and Ethiopic textual traditions • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 76 — The Twelve Portals of the Winds
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest primary-language witnesses responsibly available for this chapter. The Hasmonean-period Aramaic manuscript 4Q210 (4QEnastrᶜ ar), fragment 1 ii, is primary wherever its extant wording overlaps portions of verses 3–10 and 13–14; its surviving readings include the four healing winds, eight destructive winds, the eastern and southern portals, and the completion of the twelve gates. Lacunae in that fragment remain unsupplied. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann's 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, supplies verses 1–2 and 11–12 and the wording absent from the fragmentary Aramaic portions. The Aramaic and Geʽez forms sometimes differ in detail; the earlier legible Aramaic is followed where it survives, while the Geʽez preserves the chapter's complete sequence. No unattested wording was supplied, and no modern English translation was used as the translation base.

verses.text: At the ends of the earth I saw twelve portals standing open for all the winds. From them the winds go out and blow over the earth.
verses.study: The vision locates the winds within twelve ordered openings. Even forces that seem free and invisible are portrayed as having assigned points of departure.
crossReferences: Ecclesiastes 1:6 — the wind circles and returns on its course
Jeremiah 10:13 — God brings wind from his storehouses

verses.text: Three of them open on the face of heaven, three in the west, three on the right side of heaven and three on the left.
verses.study: The twelve portals are divided evenly across four sides. Symmetry gives the chapter a framework for distinguishing the winds and their effects.
crossReferences: Ezekiel 42:16–20 — four sides are measured in ordered proportion
Revelation 7:1 — four angels stand at the four corners holding the four winds

verses.text: The first three are toward the east, three toward the south, three after them on the left toward the north, and three toward the west.
verses.study: The four groups establish a complete circuit of east, south, north and west. Each direction will contain both a sequence and a distinct ministry.
crossReferences: 1 Chronicles 9:24 — ordered service is assigned toward the four directions
Luke 13:29 — people come from east, west, north and south

verses.text: Through four of these gates go out winds appointed for the healing of the earth and for giving it life. Through eight of them go out harmful winds; when they are sent, they destroy the whole earth, the waters, everything in them that grows, sprouts or creeps, and everything that lives on land.
verses.study: Four winds bring healing and life, while eight can damage land and water. The same ordered creation contains provision and judgment, neither of them outside command.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:1 — a wind passes over the earth as the waters subside
Hosea 13:15 — an east wind can dry springs and fountains

verses.text: First, through the first gate in the east goes out the east wind, which turns toward the south. From it come destruction, drought, heat and devastation.
verses.study: The first eastern wind carries severe effects. Direction and consequence are named together so that destructive weather is not confused with the life-giving winds.
crossReferences: Genesis 41:6 — an east wind scorches the grain
Jonah 4:8 — a scorching east wind brings distress

verses.text: Through the second, middle gate goes out the central east wind. From it come rain, fruit, life and dew. Through the third gate, toward the north, come cold and drought.
verses.study: The middle eastern gate brings rain, fruitfulness, life and dew, contrasting with the outer gates. Nearness in direction does not make every wind's work identical.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 33:13–14 — dew, deep waters and the sun sustain fruitfulness
Acts 14:17 — rain and fruitful seasons bear witness to divine kindness

verses.text: After these, the winds from the south go out through three gates. Through their first gate, which turns toward the east, goes out a hot wind.
verses.study: The sequence moves from east to south without breaking the three-gate pattern. The first southern wind is marked by heat.
crossReferences: Job 37:17 — the south wind brings heat
Luke 12:55 — a south wind signals coming heat

verses.text: Through the second, middle gate goes out the south wind called Negeb. From it come dew, rain, peace and life.
verses.study: The central southern wind brings the chapter's positive cluster of dew, rain, peace and life. Provision is described as both physical and whole-making.
crossReferences: Psalm 72:6–7 — rain and abundant peace belong together
Isaiah 44:3–4 — water and blessing cause life to spring up

verses.text: Through the third gate, toward the west, come dew, rain, locusts and destruction.
verses.study: Dew and rain appear beside locusts and destruction. Beneficial conditions do not guarantee an unmixed outcome, and the text refuses to flatten creation's complexity.
crossReferences: Joel 1:4 — successive locusts consume the land's produce
Amos 7:1–2 — locusts devour the late growth

verses.text: After it goes out the northern wind through its eastern gate, which turns toward the south. From it come dew, rain, locusts and destruction.
verses.study: The first northern gate repeats the mixed effects of the preceding portal. Repetition reinforces the measured arrangement of the winds.
crossReferences: Proverbs 25:23 — the north wind is associated with rain
Nahum 3:15–17 — locusts become an image of consuming judgment

verses.text: From the middle gate in a straight course come rain, dew, life and peace. Through the third gate in the west, which turns toward the north, come cloud, hoarfrost, snow, rain, dew and locusts.
verses.study: The middle gate again bears life and peace, while the third gathers multiple forms of cold and moisture with locusts. Each list preserves the portal's particular effects.
crossReferences: Job 37:6–10 — snow, rain and frost come under God's command
Psalm 147:16–18 — snow, frost and wind obey the divine word

verses.text: After these are the winds toward the west. Through the first gate, which turns toward the north, come dew, rain, hoarfrost, cold, snow and frost.
verses.study: The western sequence begins with a full range of cold-weather effects. The chapter records them as ordered outputs rather than random intrusions.
crossReferences: Job 38:22–23 — storehouses of snow and hail await their appointed use
Daniel 3:67–70 — dew, frost, cold and snow are summoned to bless the Lord

verses.text: From the middle gate come dew, rain, peace and blessing. Through the last gate, toward the south, come drought, devastation, burning heat and destruction.
verses.study: The last two portals sharply contrast blessing with burning devastation. Completion of the circuit holds mercy and severity in view together.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 28:12, 22–24 — rain blesses, while drought and scorching judge
James 5:17–18 — withheld and restored rain changes the life of the land

verses.text: So the twelve gates of the four winds of heaven are completed. I have shown you all their laws, all their harmful works and all their benefits, my son Methuselah.
verses.study: Enoch presents the ordered survey to Methuselah as transmitted knowledge. The winds' laws, harms and benefits must all be remembered for the account to be complete.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 6:6–7 — received instruction is passed to the next generation
Proverbs 4:1–4 — a father transmits life-giving teaching to his son

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 76 maps twelve wind portals in four groups of three. East, south, north and west provide an ordered frame for the weather that moves across land and water.

The chapter distinguishes four winds that heal and give life from eight that can harm. Rain, dew, fruitfulness and peace stand beside drought, heat, cold, locusts and devastation without confusing their effects.

The middle portals repeatedly carry beneficial winds, while neighboring portals often carry severe or mixed conditions. The pattern emphasizes particular appointments rather than treating every wind from one direction as the same.
The closing address to Methuselah makes the vision an act of faithful transmission. Enoch records laws, harms and benefits so the whole range of the winds' service can be known.

crossReferences: Genesis 8:1 — wind participates in the earth's renewal
Job 37:6–13 — weather fulfills purposes of correction, provision and mercy
Psalm 147:16–18 — frost, snow, wind and water obey God's word
Jeremiah 10:13 — wind comes from divine storehouses
Daniel 3:65–70 — winds and changing weather are called to praise
Revelation 7:1 — four winds are held at the earth's four corners
